author: William Saville

title: A Place to Put Jealousy
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The letter was folded into the shape of a bird.

It had been left on the Lanternwell notice board with my name written in careful blue ink. Inside was an invitation to spend an afternoon at Moonroot with Iroh, reviewing tea-stained maps of the old terraces. He had drawn a tiny teacup at the bottom and, beneath it, written that the invitation was entirely optional.

Maui read over my shoulder.

"A map date," he said.

"An archive visit."

"With tea."

"Those things can happen together."

He smiled. I waited for the joke. None came.

We were in Tideglass Cove a little later when he dropped the same length of rope twice. He wasn't usually clumsy with rope. That was why I noticed.

"Is your hand hurting again?"

"No."

"Then what's wrong?"

He pulled the line through the ring and tightened it much harder than he needed to.

"Nothing."

I put down the tide chart.

"Maui."

His shoulders lowered.

"Can we talk somewhere people aren't measuring knots?"

We walked to the little shelter above the sea-glass orchard. One raised bed was sprouting; the second was still bare because Fen had refused to transplant anything until the salt reading changed. The bench Greg and Maui had built sat beside the path, facing the water. It had no plaque, though Maui had carved a tiny fish beneath one armrest.

Before we reached the bench, Maui shifted into a hawk, circled once over the orchard, and landed on the roof with a flourish of feathers. The transformation wasn't necessary. I suspected it was the nearest available substitute for pacing.

When he became himself again, his grin was enormous and a little desperate.

"That was a spectacular entrance to a conversation I am going to handle very maturely."

"Is this about Iroh?"

"Wow. You ruin all my suspense."

Mini Maui jabbed a tiny finger at his chest. He brushed the tattoo aside.

"I know what we agreed," Maui said. "I know you're ethically non-monogamous, and I know you prefer polyamory. I even know I agreed to try, which was extremely noble of me."

"Generous of you."

"Legendary." The joke fell short. He looked at the garden instead of at me. "I still hate imagining someone else making you laugh in a way I don't know how to."

He didn't turn the admission into a demand. I wanted to comfort him, but I also wanted him to understand that my other relationships weren't something we were negotiating away. We sat with the discomfort between us, and he eventually nudged my shoe with his much larger one.

"So," he said, "can I be jealous and still make you dinner?"

"Absolutely."

"Great. My jealous cooking is famous."

He stood instead of sitting.

"I know about Iroh," he said.

"I know you do."

"I know about the others. We talked about being ethically non-monogamous. You told me that you prefer polyamory, and I said I wanted to try being part of your life without treating it as a race."

"You did."

"I meant it."

I waited.

"But sometimes," he admitted, "I hear that you've been invited somewhere, and part of me starts inventing a story where everybody else gets the best parts of you."

The wind lifted a strand of hair across my face.

"Which parts?"

"The ones that aren't tired from fixing the village. The ones that laugh because someone said something clever and not because you're trying to make me feel better."

His voice was almost embarrassed.

I wanted to tell him he was wrong. I wanted to assure him that I laughed more with him, or loved him more, or somehow held a private scale on which I could prove he wasn't losing.

Any of those answers would have made the feeling smaller at the cost of making somebody else's love a competition.

"I laugh with you because you're funny," I said. "Sometimes because you're ridiculous. Those are not consolation laughs."

His mouth twitched.

"Mostly ridiculous."

"Frequently."

He sat down at last.

"What do I do with this feeling? I don't want to tell you who you may see."

"You can tell me when you're afraid. You can ask for time together. You can ask whether a plan has changed. But I can't promise never to love anyone else, and I won't ask them to disappear to make us feel safe."

Maui stared at the tide.

"I don't want that either."

"I believe you."

He looked up.

"You do?"

"Yes. Wanting reassurance isn't the same thing as wanting control. It's what you do with it that matters."

He leaned back.

"That's inconvenient. I was hoping there'd be a monster to fight."

"Jealousy doesn't have claws, Maui."

"Mine might."

I laughed, and this time he laughed with me.

We sat until the breeze grew cold. I told him I could make time for a meal after my archive visit, but only if I finished when I'd said I would and didn't overpromise to Iroh. He told me he wanted us to have a day with no errands, no celebrations, and no people asking him to carry things.

"A day of doing nothing?" I asked.

"Not nothing."

"What, then?"

"Whatever we choose after breakfast."

That sounded wonderful.

We put it on the calendar.

At Moonroot, the map Iroh had invited me to see was spread beneath a weighted sheet of glass. A corner had been damaged by an old leak, leaving the ink blurred where the terrace boundaries met.

"This is what I wanted your opinion on," he said. "It appears someone redrew a garden path after the flood. I don't know whether the new route was ever used."

I studied the line. The nearest record showed an invoice for gravel, but no confirmation that the work had been done. Iroh didn't ask me to solve it with a flash of remembered knowledge. He asked which evidence we should look for next.

I thought of Maui's rope, dropped twice, and of how jealous he'd sounded without wanting to make me responsible for fixing the feeling.

"Can I tell you something without making it your problem?" I asked.

"Certainly."

"Maui was afraid I would enjoy this afternoon so much that I'd stop wanting days with him."

Iroh set his cup down. "Do you want me to reassure him?"

"No. That's between us. I wanted you to know why I might seem distracted."

He nodded. "Then we can be distracted together, briefly, and return to the map."

We sat in silence until I remembered the gravel invoice. Iroh smiled at the practical suggestion. It was one of the ways he differed from Maui: where Maui wanted to move the mountain, Iroh sometimes wanted to examine the date written at its foot.

"I like both of you," I said. "In different ways. I've been explicit that I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. I don't want either affection turned into a test the other has to pass."

"Then perhaps we should both resist the temptation to be the most reassuring person in the room."

I laughed. "You make that sound easy."

"Oh, it isn't. I am extraordinarily good at giving advice nobody requested."

He touched my hand, then waited. I leaned closer, enough to tell him the invitation was welcome. We kissed briefly beside the map table before returning to the damaged record. Neither of us claimed to have fixed jealousy or the old terrace in one afternoon.

On my way to Moonroot, I stopped at the notice board. The old departure ledger had been updated with a sign explaining how travelers could request private help leaving without surrendering their destination. Somebody had placed a bowl of chalk beside it so visitors could mark whether they'd already received assistance, then erase the mark themselves.

I thought about how much had changed since everyone treated the arrival book like a list of people the vale owned.

At Moonroot, Iroh greeted me with tea and a stack of maps.

"You look thoughtful," he said.

"Maui and I had a difficult conversation."

"Would you like to tell me?"

"Some of it."

He listened without asking me to make a comparison between them. We examined the old terrace drains, discovered a marking that might indicate a seasonal overflow, and argued gently over whether a particular line was a road or a watercourse.

When I returned to Tideglass, Maui was cooking. Properly dried kindling burned beneath a pot of vegetables, and he'd set two places at the table.

"How was your date?" he asked.

"Good. We found a possible drainage mark."

"Romantic."

"In its way."

He studied me.

"Did you have a good time?"

"Yes."

His expression softened.

"Good."

I went around the table and kissed his cheek.

He turned toward me, surprised.

"Was that a reassurance kiss?"

"No," I said. "That was a kiss because I wanted to kiss you."

"Important distinction."

"Extremely."

He asked if I wanted another.

I did.

We burned the first piece of bread because neither of us remembered the stove. Later, with dinner rescued and the windows open to the sea, he told me he'd still felt jealous for a few minutes after I left.

"And?"

"And then I went to see Fen about the ropes. I didn't make you come home early. I didn't ask Iroh to change his plans."

I took his hand.

"That sounds like a good place to put the feeling."

"Where?"

"Somewhere it can be heard without becoming the person in charge."

He considered that, then pulled me close enough that I could rest my forehead against his.

"Can I ask for something else?"

"Yes."

"That day without errands."

"It's on the calendar."

"Can it start with sleeping late?"

"Absolutely."

He grinned.

That night we closed the kitchen door, left the dishes soaking, and kept the remainder of our time private. The next morning the dishes were still there. So was the calendar.

We washed them together, and neither of us pretended we'd cured jealousy forever.
